rationale: The cited texts support the entry’s central distinction: a “work” is a deed, while its character as obedience, disobedience, wage-earning labor, or enacted faith depends on context. Exodus 18:20 directly distinguishes the laws taught from “the work” to be done; Micah 6:16 shows deeds governed by rival statutes; Romans 4:4-5 concerns work presented as a claim to wages and debt; James 2:21-22 concerns an act that brings faith to visible completion; and Luke 17:7-10 denies that even complete performance of commanded duty puts the master in the servant’s debt. The common interpretation that works are outward deeds manifesting inward allegiance is substantially compatible with this core and therefore does not furnish a contradictory alternative. The book nevertheless explains the selected contrasts more precisely by separating the deed itself from its governing authority and from any claim of merit.
book_core_identification: Works are deeds or actions, not a synonym for obedience; whether a work constitutes obedience or disobedience depends on the authority or command it enacts.
book_secondary_elaborations: Romans 4 contrasts faith with labor offered as a claim for wages, rather than contrasting faith with every form of obedience.
Abraham’s work in James 2 is the visible enactment and completion of his faith.
Even complete obedience performs an owed duty and does not earn a wage from God or place God in the servant’s debt.
The context identifies a work’s master, moral character, and whether the worker is claiming compensation.
strongest_counter_interpretation: Works ordinarily means morally significant conduct that expresses and evidences inward faith, character, or allegiance: good works are the fruit of grace and living faith, while evil works disclose unbelief or corrupt allegiance. Paul can additionally use works for attempted meritorious law-observance, but this is a contextual subtype rather than the controlling definition.
counter_core_identification: Works are outward deeds or conduct functioning as the visible fruit and evidence of inward faith, character, and allegiance.
material_core_denial: The counter does not materially deny that works are deeds distinct from obedience. At most, it resists making the governing lawgiver the principal organizing distinction and emphasizes the deeds’ evidentiary relation to inward character.
counter_case: Matthew 7:16-20 and James 2:14-26 portray deeds as fruit or evidence by which inward faith and character become known.
John 3:19-21 and Galatians 5:19-23 classify deeds by their moral source—darkness or flesh versus God or the Spirit.
Ephesians 2:8-10 distinguishes salvation from works while presenting good works as the intended fruit of grace.
Accordingly, works can often be described adequately as morally revealing conduct without an explicit inquiry into which lawgiver commanded each deed.
book_explanatory_advantages: It preserves the ordinary lexical sense of work as a deed while avoiding the false equation of every work with obedience.
It accounts for Exodus 18:20’s distinction between ordinances or laws and the work those laws require.
It explains Micah 6:16, where conduct can faithfully execute the statutes of Omri and counsels of Ahab yet be disobedient to God.
It distinguishes Romans 4’s wage-and-debt transaction from James 2’s faithful action without forcing the same soteriological function onto both uses.
Luke 17:7-10 directly supports the claim that commanded service does not create a meritorious debt.
It incorporates the common interpretation’s strongest point by treating Abraham’s work as faith made visible rather than as a purchase price for justification.
counter_explanatory_advantages: It better represents the frequent biblical emphasis on works as fruit revealing inward character or spiritual allegiance.
It applies naturally to the broad good-works and evil-works vocabulary beyond the entry’s limited citation set.
It does not require the somewhat stronger claim that every work’s status is best analyzed through the identity of a distinct lawgiver.
decisive_sources: Exodus 18:20 — distinguishes taught laws, the way to walk, and the work to be done.
Micah 6:16 — depicts works governed by the statutes and counsels of corrupt human authorities.
Romans 4:4-5 — explicitly defines the relevant working in terms of reward reckoned as debt rather than grace.
James 2:21-22 — presents Abraham’s work as cooperating with and completing faith.
Luke 17:7-10 — denies that performance of all commanded duties gives the servant a wage claim or makes the master indebted.
unresolved_objections: The claim that another “lawgiver” governs every disobedient work is more systematic than the cited texts explicitly state; evil works may also be described as arising from desire, flesh, or darkness.
Psalm 111:7 places God’s works and commandments in parallel but does not by itself prove that works are intrinsically “commandment-shaped.”
The entry’s framework is sound for the supplied texts but should not erase specialized uses such as Jesus’ miraculous works or Paul’s phrase “works of the law.”
